entities.summary:
Halime Sultan (died 1628) was a powerful Ottoman Valide Sultan, mother of Sultan Mustafa I, whose influence spanned the early 17th century, a period marked by political instability and the flourishing of the "Sultanate of Women." Her career, deeply intertwined with the reigns of her husband Mehmed III and especially her son, illustrates the profound, albeit often indirect, power wielded by imperial women within the Topkapi Palace. Operating within the rigid hierarchical structures of the Ottoman court, Halime navigated complex succession crises and factional struggles, ultimately shaping the imperial trajectory during a crucial transitional phase of the empire.

Halime's ascent to power began with her marriage to Sultan Mehmed III. Her true political prominence, however, commenced with the accession of her son, Mustafa I, in 1617. During Mustafa's initial three-month reign, and more significantly during his second, longer reign (1622–1623), Halime served as Valide Sultan and de facto regent. She wielded considerable authority, issuing imperial commands, managing the imperial harem, and influencing appointments, all while Mustafa I exhibited signs of mental instability. Her regency during Mustafa's second reign, following the deposition of Osman II, saw her collaborate closely with her son-in-law, Grand Vizier Kara Davud Pasha, to consolidate power and address the empire's burgeoning internal and external challenges.
